There were Unionist majorities of 20,000, 16,000, 14,000, I think more than that in the city of Winnipeg, overwhelming majorities. General public sentiment demands that racial dissensions between the two peoples shall stop and that large majorities because of the holding of these strong opinions shall cease, and that all the people in this country will get together to do what we know is our duty, which is the dearest hope of most of us, namely, to first uphold the honour of all Canada.
I did not notice in the speeches made by the Leader of the Opposition and his follower who so chivalrously made way for him, an invitation which was given out last year or perhaps the year before, and which had for its figurative expression " a light in the window." That was a genial invitation to return, to Liberals who had formerly been with the party which now calls itself Liberal. He said that there was a light in the window and that the latch string was on the outside of the door. It is perfectly obvious that that invitation has not had any great effect. It has brought only two of that class of members from this side of the House and they had made up their minds fairly definitely before the invitation was given. The trouble with the Liberals who were thus invited was that they were not sure of the treatment they would receive after they went back in response to the light in the window. The house was all right. We helped to build the house, but the point is that you cannot live in a house unless the coal bin is pretty full and there is enough in the larder, and we did not see any particular reasons for having a good social time in the house in which the light was put in the window. The consequence was that

there were not many defections from this side, and perhaps it is because the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) has seen the futility of repeating the invitation, or because my hon. friend who is now his leader is not of the same hospitable character as his predecessor that that invitation has not been mentioned again. It is important to refer to some extent to that, because I think that it is a proper time now after two years, that I should make some observations regarding the first of the cleavages which we saw two years ago.
Political cleavages in parties are not unknown in Canada. They have generally occurred owing to a large mass of the people of one party hoping for commercial advantages, or on the other hand, because of some religious question which has stirred the hearts of the people. The Liberal Party and the Liberal Government of 1878 lost thousands and thousands of supporters who thought that their commercial welfare would be better served by more Protection, and the great majority of those supporters never came back to the party. The Conservative party in 1896 lost a very considerable number of its supporters, who objected that the Dominion Government was interfering with the rights of a province in the matter of separate school education. There we have an example, in the first place, of commercial advantage, and in the second place, of religious fervour, which are the two chief causes of cleavages in parties. Then we come to 1917, when for the first time we had a great world war, which was more potent than any other factor in creating cleavages in parties. It is true that some of us had to separate from our old friends, and we have been referred to as " The prodigal son," as the boy who has strayed away, or, setting the theme to music, " Oh, Where is My Wandering Boy To-night?" But it must be remembered that it wTas not only one boy who left the old home, but most of the boys. Anyway, "the" boys, the best boys, left the party because of its policy in connection with the carrying on of the war. If you will look at the election results you will see that the vast majority of the Liberals who could not follow their old party on this issue were elected without the help of the military vote. If you look at the other side of the House you will find that only two Liberals were elected in Ontario, the greatest and most populous province in Canada, on what might be called old party lines, and the others come from constituencies in which, for racial reasons,

feeling was aroused to a very great extent against Great Britain. I am not competent to speak of other provinces, but as a general result the vast majority of the Liberal-Unionists candidates were elected. We on this side of the House cannot object to those who are left calling themselves the Liberal Party if they like, because everybody has the right to call himself whatever he chooses, but it does seem absurd that those who are in the minority should attempt to make out that we have not been treated properly on this side of the House, and that we have been absorbed into a party by another name. As a matter of fact, while we have been over here we have been well received. We have found no attempt at proselytizing. Our opinions have been received with civility, and furthermore, we have found something that has amazed us, and which would have amazed some of my hon. friends opposite had they come over here, and that is that there are more real Liberals on this side of the House than there are on the other. I will go further. I have found men on this side of the House who call themselves Conservative for party reasons, who are more radical than any I have ever found among my old friends the Liberals. I have been astounded to learn of the uprooting that some alleged Tories on this side of the House were willing to do in one way or another, so one is naturally bound to come to the conclusion that these old party names stand for nothing when a great cataclysm comes and a man takes the course he thinks is right. I am quite aware that the so-called Liberals, if they will not mind my using that term,-anyway, the Liberals,- have been saying disagreeable things, as they have a right to do, about defections and turn-overs, but I can assure them that there is nothing on this side of the House that has given offence to those Liberals who went out for the principles of which I have spoken. Not only have we been well received, but we have heard nothing of the extreme views which my hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) attributes to our colleagues on this side of the House. They have not tried to rub in, so to speak, their own particular opinions. I have heard that there are some strong party men on this side, just as there are strong party men on the other side of the House, who would prefer to be alone, but, of course, they have been civil enough not to let us find that out, except that we have heard some reference here to-day to certain efforts of a former Cabinet minister hailing from Winnipeg. So far as our colleagues on this side of the House, are concerned, we have had very pleasant relations with those with whom we formerly disagreed.
The war changed things in many ways, and with the exception of those who had the most tense political feelings and political inclinations, the war made men think as they wanted to think without regard to political party trammels.
It is proper for me now, I think, after two years, and as the subject has never been discussed in Parliament before, to give a short history of the rise of the cleavage in the Liberal party, and I can do it best, and it seems to me it would be the most convincing to those who are listening to me, by giving my own personal experience. In September, 1917, returning from my usual summer vacation, when one does not read many newspapers, I was surprised to find that there were some people in the country who were opposed to Canada taking further part in the great war. I discussed this matter with three men of political prominence, candidates under the leadership of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and I expressed my views, because I held them definitely and strongly. I said " We cannot let Canada down now that we have sent her in; we cannot let our boys at the Front get discouraged and weaken; we have-to send more men." The first man replied, " Of course we should, but what has that to do with politics?" Then he told me he had been going around among the people and had found that conscription was unpopular, and that Conservatives who did not want their sons to go to the Front were going to vote for the Liberal party if the Conservative party stood for conscription. The next man, who was also a candidate, agreed that many Conservatives who did not want their sons to go to the Front would vote for the Liberal party to avoid conscription, and he gave instances to show that conscription was not going to win. These men were of that type. I shall not mention their names, but I am not abusing any confidence because anything which they said to me they will say at any time. They thought that while it was proper for Canada to continue her effort in the war, as was done afterwards by the Union Government, the more important thing was that the Liberals should get into power. That disposes of two from whom I got opinions. The third to whom I spoke-a candidate afterwards-rather shocked me when he said: "Well, I think we have done enough; let Uncle Sam do the rest." Well, I do not care to express

contempt for any man, but if ever I felt like doing so in my life it was on the occasion of this assertion. If these be candidates of the Liberal party, 1 felt, how is it possible for us, who think differently from them, to march in double harness with them again unless they change their minds? We could not endorse any policy of nonsupport of our men who were in the war and so there was an election. Now, mark this: The Liberals who left their party were as convinced as those who remained in it that conscription was an unpopular issue. They thought that they would be defeated, but apprehension of defeat did not alter their intention and determination that the war should be fought to a successful issue. Fo it came about, in an imposing outburst of public enthusiasm, that the Union Government, which was pledged to continue the war, was sustained except in one province. None were more surprised than the Liberals who had run as candidates in support of the Union Government, and I must say that the result was gratifying to them. When a prominent member on the other side made a remark in Ottawa last winter that the Liberals who left their party had done so for their personal aggrandisement I assured him he was wrong. We were elected through the patriotism of the people, in Ontario at any rate; but at the time we ran there was no idea of personal gain -at all. We had played the political game before, but on that occasion we claim that we played the game of what was right for Canada without regard to the political party to which we belonged. I therefore give no credit to men like the three of whom I have spoken; they were wrong in their heads as well as in their hearts. They made a bad guess politically. They thought they were going to win and they lost, and I give them no credit for possessing any right principle or anything else to boast of. It was a pure political game with them. As I say, they were of opinion that they would win, but they lost; and it now ill becomes them to throw slurs at those who thought or acted differently from them.
I shall now conclude by saying that while this is not a political party on this side of the House-most of us have voted against the Government repeatedly, although the Government has not been sensitive on that point, knowing that our hearts and our allegiance were generally in the right place -while we are not a party, 1 do not see why we should not become one. Men of like opinions, men with the same ideals in re-

gard to the future of Canada, men who do not wish to see racial dissension or cleavage in the country, if they can meet on this side for two years and have no serious disagreement as to what is needed for good government, regardless of former party shibboleths, may very well compose a party. While therefore we are not yet a party, if there is any proposal that we should become a party and the leaders can devise a policy consistent with the ideals I ha\ e seen on this side, I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the Liberal-Unionists are going to join that party. We are assured there will be nothing new which will be inconsistent with anything we were ever told in political meetings on the liberal si te. I ask my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King; now seriously-nay, humourously-did he ever hear political principles of a liberal kind discussed in a Liberal political meeting? No, he did not. Well, neither did I. We always played the party game. We were party men; and what a lot of rot it is to talk about Liberal principles or Conservative principles all the time! We were party men. But sometimes in a crisis we cannot be party men, and if we can find something better to substitute for what exists there is no reason why we should not take it. And we will take it. I, in common with the Liberals on this side, have had pleasure in supporting this Government, and supporting it enthusiastically, even though it be unpopular. During war I do not want to support a Government merely because it is popular. I want to support a Government that does the right thing even if it is going to be unpopular. And what a number of unpopular things this Government has had to do! One thing after another, which would almost strain to breaking point the ordinary man, these men in the Government benches, heedless of party politics, caring not whether their actions might incur the disapproval of their supporters or constituencies, or what effect those actions might have in the event of an election, have day in and day out framed policies and passed measures-Orders in Council, if you will- that were bound to be unpopular, but which were in their belief for the ultimate good of the country. The only thing that saved Canada during the war was the fact that there was a Government that was not afraid to do things that would be unpopular. And I mistake very much the temper and the generous spirit of my fellow-countrymen if they will not ultimately support a body of men such as compose the present

Government. It is true that at the present juncture criticism is freely indulged in. Attacks are made in every quarter; everyone is abusing everyone else-the Bolshevists condemn the Government. The returned soldiers abuse the pacifists. But when this state of feeling subsides, I have enough faith in my fellow-countrymen and enough confidence in their gratitude to know that they will support the party that did the right thing whether it was popular or not. I admit there is some talk of the unpopularity of the Government at the present moment, but that does not bother me a bit, because we know that it is merely a passing cloud. While it is fostered by my friends on the other side-sometimes, I regret to say, not altogether fairly-I know it is but transient. And when the next election comes, whether at the time demanded in my friend's motion, or a little later-probably a little later-the present Government, comprising men who formerly held different political views, is going to be swept ultimately into power again. The history of Canada shows that the people have favoured keeping governments a long time in power during the last forty years, and history will repeat itself at the next election. Then, my hon. friends, I think, will be somewhat ashamed of themselves when they go down to defeat-except in one province-because they did not try to unite with us to put an end to dissension, to throttle the racial feeling the moment it appeared, and to lend their support to a government working for the advantage of the whole country and of the whole Empire, and for the well-being of mankind at large.

Mr. Speaker, it is
my intention to speak in my own language on this occasion but before entering upon any remarks I wish to answer very briefly the speaker'who has just preceded me (Mr. Mowat). The hon. gentleman says that we are not ready for an election and he concluded his remarks by stating that whenever there should be an appeal to the people the Government he is supporting would come back triumphantly to power. If it is true that we are not ready for an election, and if the Government is sure to come back triumphantly to power, why do they refuse the amendment of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition 5 p.m. (Mr. King)? We do not ask a dissolution because we hope to come back to power; we ask a dissolution in order that the people shall have an opportunity to say whether or not they have
any confidence in this Government. We do not care to come back to power but we want to fulfil our duty. That is the difference between us and the hon. gentleman. He says also that now is the time to try and get nearer to the province of Quebec. Speaking in my own name, and for my province, I will quote the words of one of our public men who says that the province of Quebec is not in a state of mind to enter into any conference; it has been misjudged; it has been badly treated; it has been slandered; it is waiting for its hour and after that it will confer but not before.
The hon. gentleman says that whenever the Government shall be ready to propound a policy, that policy will appeal to the people of Canada. Yesterday the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government (Sir George Foster) told us that they liad a policy but the hon. member for Parkdale who supports this Government is not aware that there is a policy. He tells us that there is going to be a policy propounded and in advance he tells the country that he is going to support it. I believe he is a bad supporter of the present Administration as he was a bad supporter of the Liberal party. If he desires to come back to the Liberal fold we will receive him because the door is open, but if he should be only as good a supporter of the Liberal party as he is of this Government we will not rely very much upon him. I will now proceed with my remarks in my own language.

Mr. Speaker, the mover of the address in answer to the speech from the Throne told us that the war had destroyed the old order of things political in this country and that Canada was entering into a new era. That is exactly what we believe, that is precisely what we maintain and that is also what the leader of the Liberal party, the leader of the Opposition, has submitted to this House and to the country in moving for the dissolution of Parliament.
He laid emphasis on the fact that the hybrid alliance which gave birth to the government we have been enjoying since 1917 had brought about the overturn of the old political order of things.
What is the present situation and how did it originate? For the winning of the war, the constitution of the country had to be battered in; to win the war, individual righto had to be done away with; to win the war, the constitution had to be

suspended; individual sacrifices had to be appealed to, in order to achieve victory and bring to a triumphant conclusion the cause supported by the Allies. These hon. gentlemen that sit on the Treasury benches maintained that, in order to have a free hand and plenty elbow room, all the existing laws had of necessity to be suspended and the Parliament oif this country had to give up its prerogatives, so as to hand over to ministers sitting in the Unionist cabinet the full control of public affairs.
Aware as we are that, in order to build up that Unionist party and that Union government, all men of good will had to be appealed to; when we call to mind that sincere Liberals, for the time being, severed connection with and cut loose from their *party to join hand in hand with men they had hitherto opposed, it is most regrettable to find that the acting .Prime Minister of this country has deemed it fit to slap them in the face, as he did yesterday. How so, Sir? The Acting Prime Minister told us that in 1917, not only was the Unionist party elected on the platform of prosecution of the war, but that the new allies had agreed on (a political programme, and that the election of 1917 was won not only to carry the war to a victorious conclusion, but on a well-defined political programme. Is there a single individual, out of this House, who is going to believe-for in this House under our rules, one is bound to accept the statements made by an hon. member from his seat, and so far as I ,am concerned, I am bound, so long as I sit here, to believe that the Acting Prime Minister did really make a statement borne out by the facts- but let- me ask the hon. members who sit within these precincts whether 'there is a single individual, outside this House, when not bound by the rules of the House, who would believe that my -hon. friend, the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. W. S. Fielding), a former Prime Minister of his province, one of the outstanding figures of the Liberal party, .a minister of Finance for fifteen yearns, who has waged war on the protection 'tariff so dear to the hearts of these gentlemen, who is the man, I say, who is going to believe that the hon. member for iShelburne and Queen's did really come to an understanding with the Acting Prime Minister on a well defined political programme previous to the election? Had such an understanding been reached, how happens it that my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's severed his connection with and cut loose from the Unionist party, and returned to the 
party fold, sitting now in the ranks of the Liberal Opposition?
In the reference to the words fallen from the lips of the Acting Prime Minister, and directed to those colleagues of his who supported him in times of stress, it strikes me that it was paying them a very poor compliment to say that they proved false to and have gone back on the pledges given prior to the election of 1917. By no means, Sir. Who is going .to believe that the hon. member from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) did really forswear his allegiance 'to free trade, in order to .adhere and subscribe to a prearranged political platform of the hon. gentlemen? Who is going to be fooled into believing that the former Minister of Agriculture who is now sitting alongside the representatives of the United Farmers, and old .Liberals, old oppositionists to the present Government, had joined the Union government with a well defined political programme?
Oh no ! these gentlemen may well try to throw .duet in 'the eyes of the people, they may well try to belittle the grandeur of those who, in a moment of distress, believed in the sincerity of the scattered remnants of the Tory party,, believed at a time that really their help was necessary to enroll the live forces of the nation, to enlist our youth and send 500,000 of our sons to the battlefields of Europe, while draining the wealth of the country; of such men as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, as the hon. member for Red Deer, as my hon. friend the member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) who, in a manner to which I will later call attention, has just left the government which he had joined. These men had believed that their help was necessary, and because they believed that their help was necessary I bow to them for the course they took; I recognize that they obeyed the dictates of their conscience. But, after having accomplished the work for which they had abandoned their party, when they think proper to come back to that party, it seems to me that they deserve other treatment at the hands of those whom they have .helped to retain power, that they deserve other treatment than to be told that when they entered the Government there was a perfectly definite political programme which they deserted before its realization.
I am bound to believe that there was a programme, but I doubt very much whether the public will give much credence to this statement of the Acting Prime Minister.
It is said that there exists a general uneasiness in the country. To this the

Acting Prime Minister answers, well, the cost of living hais risen in all countries, we suffer as they suffer elsewhere. This is no answer. Mr. Speaker, allow me to point out a clear proof of the uneasiness which obtains in the country. You see at the end of the benches, oni your left, men who sit in this House aloof from the parties. Why have they been elected to this House? What is the reason of their aloofness? The reason is that there exists at this moment in the country an intense uneasiness caused by the faulty legislation, by the scandalous administration, of the present Government. The people are looking about in search of a remedy. These United Farmers of Ontario, who have awakened the political hopes of the farmers of Canada, on what have they built their hopes? These political hopes are born of contempt for broken promises; they are born of the fact that a Minister of Militia, in the first days of December 1917, with a view to capturing, the votes of the farmers' sons and of the farmers of Ontario, went over that province exhibiting an Order in Council, and declaring that he, the Minister of Militia, had obtained it so that the sons of farmers would never go to the war. The election took place. The Unionist party was returned. And the result was that immediately after the proclamation of the vote, the farmers' sons were called to arms notwithstanding the Order in Council, which had been repealed in spite of the promise of this Minister.
And you wonder now that among the people, when men holding public offices are capable, in, order to gain a momentary success, of making game of the public confidence, of treading under foot their promises and their oaths, you are astonished that there is uneasiness?
Well, the uneasiness is taking shape. To-day it is to be seen in the claims of the farmers grouping themselves into a unit, and deciding that henceforth neither the party in power nor the party in opposition are capable of satisfying their hopes and their ambitions. And as is the ease for all class1 movements, the responsibility for this movement rests upon the Government, by reason of their policy, their legislation and their administration.
The greatest crime with which I reproach those who sit on the ministerial benches, is of having started in this country this movement, which is setting classes against each other and stirring up throughout the country a turmoil of which no one may foretell the consequences.
The uneasiness is wide spread, you say; yes, it is, and it is becoming more and
more so. And, Sir, what comforts me now is to see that in the maelstrom which draws in province after province,, in this orgy of folly, of destruction which rouses province against province, which rouses race against race, regions, classes, against each other, alone the province of which I am one of the representatives, remains at its work, continues to love the soil, continues to cherish its institutions and, notwithstanding the abuse which has been heaped upon it, gives its calumniators, its persecutors the example of true patriotism, by remaining attached to the soil, intent upon work, and developing energy, in order to bring about the production which is so much needed. That is the answer to the slanders and insults cast upon the province of Quebec.
The right hon. Acting Prime Minister used an unfortunate expression, when, speaking of the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition, he called it '"camouflage". If the action of the leader of the Liberal party may be termed camouflage,, there is a stand of the Government which I look upon as deserving much more to be so characterized.
I know that within these precincts it is rather difficult to speak openly, but I shall not disguise my thoughts, whatever the outcome. If there be any camouflaging, it is in representing the Prime Minister of this country as being so broken in health as to prevent his taking his seat in this House for the last three sessions, and in saying that he requires two different kinds of attendants, for the Prime Minister, since his stay in Europe,, has developed an immoderate liking for international and foreign affairs. Therefore he has an attendant for external affairs and until recently had two more for the home policies.
As regards external affairs, I am bound, as I said a moment ago, to take the hon. Acting Prime Minister's word and to acknowledge that the Prime Minister is sick, and that is the sole reason for his not being present. But can you possibly imagine that the people will believe that the Prime Minister is so ill that he cannot attend to the business of Parliament when they hear that he has gone away on an imperial mission with Lord Jellicoe to establish naval forces in all the colonies of the Empire? If he is too ill to come to this Parliament how is it that they throw upon him the burden of discussing the naval policy.
We cannot believe that /Lord Jellicoe took Sir Robert Borden away with him simply on account of his own personality. Nobody would believe that, because Lord Jellicoe

has other business to do than that of looking after a sick man. He simply took Sir Robert Borden with him because he is Prime Minister of Canada. Here is a man who, according to the description given by the Acting Prime Minister, is unable to follow the sittings of this House and who, however,, is being overburdened with the consideration of the whole naval policy. But that is not all. Our Prime Minister comes back to the American continent, he calls at Halifax and immediately upon his arrival at New York, he is met by his two attendants for home affairs who discuss with him during two days the policy which is to be adopted by the Government of this Dominion.
I always thought that public life involved for those who entered it, the sacrifice of every hope of home life, of their profession or business in favour of the common weal. But I never fancied that when a public man became ill, everybody should strive to hasten his death. Such a thought never occurred to me. However it seems to be the case; if we are to believe the statements made by the right hon. gentleman from the oppoisite side of the House. Here is a sick and feeble man who,, according to press reports and conversations among his friends, is gone to South Africa when he has not actually reached New7 York, who has arrived in Florida when he is still aboard Lord Jellicoe's ship, who is supposed to be in New York and is found the next day in London, who when reported to be still in London is in Halifax and in New York when they look for him in Halifax. Nobody can see him. It is jugglery, witchcraft, camouflage.
I was never a supporter of the Prime Minister, but had I been one of his friends,. I think I should have treated him better than his so-called friends do to-day. I should have shown some compassion, even for the sake of decency if he were not sick. But personally I believe he is ill, because the hon. Acting Prime Minister gave us his word and we have to take it.
Now there is one observation the people will not fail to make. The leader of the Opposition, as in duty bound, moved an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the Throne, asking for the immediate dissolution of this Parliament, on the ground that it does not, and neither does the present Government, represent the people.
The right honourable Acting Prime Minister calls that strategy, though suspecting it

is rather camouflage. Then the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) is sure that the Liberal Opposition is not ready for the fray and that if we had an election in the near future the present Government would be returned by an immense majority. I take *for granted the statement made by the acting Prime minister that ithe 'Government cannot agree with the strategic move of the Opposition. The Government and their supporters will go to the people with the same platform upon which they were elected in 1917 and the member for Parkdale says that if we had an election to-morrow the Opposition would be crushed.
Well we fully realize the bearing of hon. gentleman's argument. We are perfectly well aware that the Liberal party, in order to live up to its war 'time obligations, suffered the Government to encroach upon the prerogative of Parliament, upon the rights of the representatives of the people, upon the franchises of the people; and we realize that public opinion instead of giving us credit for such sacrifices and generosity, and because it has been poisoned by a salaried press, is under the impression that the Opposition is not any better than the Government. In spite of this and of the agitation of the united farmers and of the efforts of the Government to hold on to power, notwithstanding what may happen, we are ready to take a risk. And why? Because above the Unionist, Farmers' or Liberal parties there lies the public interest. We much prefer that a new parliament should be the outcome of the election, a house truly representative of the people and conducting the affairs of the country according to the wishes of the people and in the interest of the people, rather than our being returned to power and taking Sir Robert Borden's heritage, which is far from being enviable.
The Opposition may well take a pride in their action. iStill that which denotes broadness of mind, and magnanimity is greeted by our opponents with unkindness and contempt. Whatever the Union party may-say or do, we shall have to go back to the form of responsible government, to the government by the people. Personally I think there is nothing more pitiful in what is going on under our eyes in Canada at the present time than the fact of the acting Prime Minister being forced to defend an indefensible case and being absolutely unable to make his views prevail. It is not customary with me to praise my opponents, but as far as the right hon. Acting Prime

Minister is concerned, I think he fully understands the bearing of our leader's declarations. He realized his position was a difficult one and accordingly marshalled all the resources of his imagination, all his expertness in dialectics and parliamentary training. May I be allowed to state that he sorely disappointed us? It is not surprising. .Such an accomplishment exceeded even his means and resourcefulness. The stand taken by the Opposition is unassailable, but that which the Government forces the Acting Prime Minister to defend is anti-constitutional and inimical to the principles of responsible government. No one in this House knows it better than the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government in 'the absence of one who ought to be here to-day.
May we not entertain the hope that in the councils of a party which boasts of having attracted the best brains in the country, there will be among its leaders some one who, in order to preserve our system of responsible government,, will impress upon the minds of those who do not understand, the danger of so jeopardizing the existence of our representative institutions.
At first the people may take no particular interest in the matter, but'to-morrow they will grumble; then unrest sets in and in the course of events which are shaping themselves you will reap what you are sowing to-day.
Whatever the Government may say or do, nobody believes that they represent the people or that they were elected through a franchise which represented public opinion. Nobody believes it. They may say: We have a sound and well balanced Government. But they are alone to say so and I think they do not even believe what they say. How could the taxpayers and those who have made sacrifices, who have contributed money and the blood of their children towards ensuring victory to the Allies, how could these people, I ask, believe it?
But the people of this country are going to call these men to a strict account for their administration of public affairs.
Besides, Sir, one need not be a great scholar to know that no administration that has comte into (office 'in war time succeeds in remaining in power after peace has come in. Why, Sir? A state of war means the destroying of all that has been painfully built up in the piping times of peace; a state of war spells the suspension of fundamental laws; a state of war involves 5
for the citizens of a country the obligation of giving up their interests, of renouncing their egotism, of sacrificing everything to the public weal. Do you believe that such sacrifices may be imposed on a whole people without a reaction being bound to arise at a given moment? Moreover, every body knows than when war is let loose, public expenditure cannot be controlled as it should be. There are uncontrollable expenditures, which go on increasing by leaps and bounds; appetites get sharpened, passions spring into flame, love of money increases and to satisfy the rank and file of the party, to gratify friends, inroads are made deeper and deeper into the public treasury, and meanwhile, public anger keeps roaring and gathering. And prior to its being let loose, torrent-like, over the country, jeopardizing those institutions for which our ancestors so long struggled, for which, I say, men of the generation of the acting Prime Minister have so often done battle and for which institutions those who .will come after us are willing to live, struggle and contend, so as to improve and enlarge them, were it not high time we told the Government: In the public interest, gentlemen, do not hesitate to sink your personal ambitions,, to make up your mind to renounce the sweets of office, go to the country, appeal to the people, and should the people, through means I do not wish to qualify here, wish to give you another lease of power, you shall at least have public 'Confidence behind you, you shall at least have the support of public opinion. Beware you do not tarry and wait till class feeling has reached such a pitch that you can no longer stem the tide. The farming community, in this country, should it syndicate, would prove to be the power par excellence, and you should have class legislation, an administration prejudicial to public development. And this, because of your refusing, at a given moment, to take up a position which your duty to the public demanded, and because of your lack of confidence in the people, who put their trust in those who have served them well.
And that is why I cannot understand the position taken by the Government in refusing to accept the amendment moved by my hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition.
The hon. member for London (Mr. H. Crony11)-and this will be my concluding remark-said in his speech in moving the Address in answer to the speech from the Throne that the state of war bad brought about the overturn of the old order of things political. I am going t-o lay down



here a .principle, 'at the risk of shocking those who hear me. I make no bones about saying that I am .a party man; II am not ashamed of stating that I am a believer in political parties and I .shall tell you why I believe in political parties. Without any political parties in which men of all classes and conditions ,may meet and give personal bickerings their quietus, so as to work harmoniously and hand in hand in the common interest, you shall have a Government made up of factions, you shall have an administration carried out by coteries or groups. Oif the two governments, that which has been most subservient to the interests of humanity, is party government. Because the government of countries carried out by political parties has proved the greatest agency for good in the world, I am still in favour of that government. I 1am still a party politician and I believe-any contrary opinion notwithstanding-that there is .magnanimity in the fact of a man who, holding strong views, tries to have them prevail, but yielding to his colleagues whose opinion runs counter to his own, is broadminded enough to .pocket his personal grievances, so that the opinions of the majority of his party friends may prevail. It strikes me that there is magnanimity in such an attitude. Do not call it servilism, do not call it slavery. Every one is entitled to hold his own opinion, until the majority has spoken, and in such a case it is the opinion of .a whole party which is voiced by the majority, and everybody must subscribe to it.
I wish to make an appeal to my right hon. friend, the .acting 'Prime Minister, because, I believe, he is a party roan, and because II invoke the statements of the supporters of this 'Government, that for the winning of the war, all political parties had to sink their differences, in order to form a coalition government, and now that the war is over, I appeal to him,-not as a political opponent,-but I am entitled to make that appeal because he is the oldest representative of the people in this House, the most experienced man, and he is considered as the strongest man in his party: let him do his best so that we may go back to the administration of public affairs in this country on the lines of well defined political parties, leaving to each group the care of urging its claims, but without giving rise to the creation of clans or classes which would bring about class and faction legislation, which would result in the overthrow of every thing we hold dear, for which we

have fought so long, and which we have inherited from our ancestors.
Before taking my seat, let me thank this House for having so long listened to my remarks, which may have proved devoid of interest to the majority of my colleagues; but I thought that under the circumstances, I was entitled to the use of my mother tongue, as the assertion of a right, and in speaking in my own name as well as on behalf of those I represent here, I wanted the claims, demands and grievances of my constituents to be heard on the floor of this House in their own mother tongue.

I should like to join Mr. Speaker, in the praise extended to the mover and seconder of the Address, for I am sure their speeches are worthy of every enconium that has been bestowed on them.
This noble building one might expect to inspire noble thoughts, but I have boen somewhat disturbed by the speech of the hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Gauthier). He began by repudiating the conciliatory remarks of the member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat), and ended, as I understood him, by saying-and he asserted that he spoke for himself and his Province-that Quebec would not confer until her hour had come, and then she would be prepared to confer. If that is what the hon. gentleman said and if that is what he meant, I would ask him if he intended that as a threat.
It is not a threat; it is a declaration.
The difference between a threat and a declaration, especially a declaration of that kind, is that the man who makes the declaration is afraid to back it up.
The hon. gentleman has no right to insinuate that I am a coward.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would not be in order for any hon. member to impute cowardice to another. It is a question of construction as to whether that is what the hon. member (Mr. Burnham) meant in the present instance, and I can hardly go so far as to place that interpretation upon his words.

Mr. Speaker, I of course bow to your ruling instantly. I might explain that I was not attributing physical cowardice to the hon. gentleman; I was attributing to him moral cowardice, something that he himself-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has now clearly brought himself within the rule of the order, and his latter remark ought to be withdrawn.

I certainly withdraw the remark, Mr. Speaker. Proceeding then upon a declaration which is not a threat, but which is a full, plain and explicit declaration by a man who is speaking for himself and his Province, as he said, I must say that I am unable to distinguish between his remarks and something of a very warlike and threatening character. I do not understand such talk as that. I am an admirer of the French. I like the French-the French of Canada as well as the French of old France. But in these days when we in Ontario have had to stand the Nationalists, when we have had to endure from Quebec every insult under Heaven, why should we be subjected to a statement of the most mysterious character, a statement that they would only confer when their hour had come. That means when their hour has struck. Well, if it means that, I can only say, with most infinite regret, that I do not care a brass farthing whether they threaten or whether they do not, for I am confident that we will be able to hold our own with equanimity.
I may say that we will never confer with the hon. gentleman, for if we did he would not understand.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

However, this sort oi feeling that has been aroused, to my infinite astonishment and very great regret indeed, seems to be in the air. The passion displayed by the gentleman of that portion of the Opposition is no doubt largely aroused through the feeling that they have lost the major portion of themselves. The farmers of this country beyond all doubt, according to my way of thinking, owe to the Liberal party, who held the fort for many a long day, at least a tribute of respect, if not of consideration. But now the farmers have repudiated the Liberal party, and surely if the farmers repudiate their associates, the least we on this side can do is to agree with them. They know the Liberals better than we do, and they have cast them aside like a brand into the burning. I regret this parting from old associates, from those who remain of a great historic party, now about to disappear because it is to be swallowed up in that far greater movement known as the Agrarian or Farmers' Movement.
This is one of those incidents arising from furious feeling which has been developed by the war. We have other exemplifications of force; we have the women of this country (whose forte is practical but not philosophical idealism), advocating force. Strange to say in this general convulsion after the war, when peace should have supervened, we have the doctrine of force being preached from one end of the country to the other, by ministers in the pulpit and by women out of it. The religion and the morals of the people, as well as their peace and content, depend upon individual liberty, and if we are to understand, as the Rev. Doctor Bland said recently in his pulpit-a prominent pulpit in Toronto-that individual liberty has disappeared, and that we must henceforth have only community liberty, then we must bow to force. Well, we will bow to force only when we have to. And we will not submit to the force of the majority, because I have known a minority that, when it came to force, could overcome a majority; and if our women and the pulpiteers have so far forgotten their respect to God, and preserve their desire to spread infidelity throughout this country, as they are most certainly doing, let them remember that the remnant who hold dear all the old basic elements of the moral law, the basis of religion, will adhere to these elements when these people proclaim, as they are proclaiming, that the death of Christ himself was unnecessary if the Almighty had had brains enought to prohibit the source of evil. It is one of the most extraordinary and deplorable conditions imaginable. I am well aware that those who say that do not mean it, but they do not know. Those people who pooh-pooh philosophy ; who sneer at the fundamental reasons of things and set up something that they adore and that they are determined to back up 'by force, have intensified the spleen and excitement which we now see throughout the country and which will result in the country's downfall if something is not done to prevent it. I am not now referring to any particular brand of prohibition. It is not necessary to stop at alcohol; that form of prohibition is a very minor affair. We need only follow that idea up to rveive at once the conditions of the inquisition. It it is wrong to misuse alcohol, it is wrong to misuse religion-and we have all the horror of the days when women were executed as witches and when people were burned at the stake, the persecutors maintaining the while a remarkable self complacency. The descendants of these very

people are to-day del girted to see a repetition of what has happened before. One cannot look hack on those days without wondering how these things could have been done; but when people are wedded to force they can' do anything. I can only say that I do not come of a race that submits to force. If force has to be exercised, then let us "cry havoc and let loose the dogs of war." We can all join in that, and possibly out of this extraordinary condition of things there may come that spirit of re-union which the hon. member for St. Hy-acintbe (Mr. Gauthier) a few moments ago seemed to repudiate. We cannot and we will not put up with this dogmatism which has been engendered by a false system of ethics, this force which has been substituted for the old religion and which sooner or later will destroy the very foundations of society.
One of the disturbing elements of the present day is, beyond all doubt, the condition of the mind of the soldier. He is not satisfied. Why? Because broadly before him is placed this simple fact: That the people Who stayed at home have profited and that the people who went to war have lost. They simply say to themselves: Upon us has fallen not only the burden of the war at the front, hut the burden of the war at home; we are ignored; we must struggle. The 'consequence is that there has been engendered and aroused a feeling which is regrettable in the extreme because it is caused by ingratitude-above all things the basest and the meanest flaw in the human chai acter.
I confess that the people who have been engaged in looking after the returned soldier have thought that they were doing well. To some extent they have been doing well. But he gives twice who gives quickly, and they did not give quickly, nor did they follow up what they intended to do with that instantaneous and practical carrying out of the intention which would have taken away so much from the sting of the loss which these men had suffered. Delay followed delay. Impracticable things were suggested. It was suggested that returned soldiers should go upon the farm who did not know a farm when they saw it. Men were offered inducements to go upon the farm but no inducements to go into business. Afterwards the loan principle was extended in some degree to business but there has been throughout a lack of promptitude on the part of our people-on the part of all of us-with regard to the soldier. And the soldier feels it. He does not want

to be paid for what he did. He cannot be paid; no country could pay him. But after four or five years of war he finds that he is in an extremely bad condition in many cases-a poor, unfortunate condition- and he thinks that if he had some decent help in time of need; if the people of this country had been a " very present help in time of trouble," this post-war period would have been tided over, with possibly few exceptions. But the condition has been so widespread and so general that it has occasioned at last a suspicion in the minds of the people themselves that all is not right. In England they have said that war fortunes must not only be regretted; they must be given up. How frequently do we say that people in this country made a good thing out of the war; but we let them keep it. Let them in all honesty and ourselves in all honour remember that while they are entitled to a fair reward and fair remuneration, they are most decidedly not entitled to keep the fortunes they made during the absence in the field of strife of our glorious soldiers. There can be and will be no satisfaction so long as these evidences of luxury are paraded before the men who made the sacrifice which made possible the enjoyment of these luxuries. Therefore when we analyze the various causes of discontent we must remember that we have not by any means done all that we could do to allay it.
The high cost of living is founded upon the most awful inflation that ever took place in the history of the world. It is true that the nations' holdings of gold have been enormously increased, but the paper currency in circulation, based upon that gold, has been still more enormously and disproportionately increased. The increase has extended from three times what it was before the war in some cases to ten times what it was before the war in others. There is an immensity of paper money. In some quarters it is worth nothing; in other quarters it is worth little, and we have high prices, based, of course, upon this inflated currency-the Governments of the world, not excluding our own Government, meanwhile standing by and taking no steps or adopting no measures to shrink that inflation and enable prices to get back to where they were. The most extraordinary feature of it all is that we have in exchange a loss to this country which is almost beyond belief and is almost more than we can bear. There are people, the farmers included, who view this condition with equanimity. They may he a little dis-

turbed, but they say: We will not buy in Canada if we can buy more cheaply out of it. Well, if they are determined to follow that system and they are bled year by year many millions of dollars in discount or by way of foreign premium, then, just as a case of Bright's disease will sooner or later destroy and exhaust a human being, so will the payment of that money surely destroy Canada. The nations of this world are not one. We have all our households, national and domestic to look after. Our farmers are the most cultured and, generally speaking, the happiest and most prosperous class in the whole community. For them to consider that they have a right to envy the rest of us because of our superior luxuries or attainments is a serious and sad mistake. I know of nowhere that the farming community enjoys such a high, broad and luxurious life as in Canada. Therefore, it is with the utmost regret that I see that they have formed themselves on a basis of force into a class or group, and to prove that they have formed themselves into an exclusive group, they say that nobody but a farmer can join them. You have nothing left; you cannot follow in behind them because you approve or disapprove their principles, because they repudiate you. And why do they repudiate you? Because their whole new policy is founded on selfishness or self interest. How can they say that they intend to do what is best for Canada when they refuse to let good Canadians join them unless they are actual farmers? They hope, by the power of their number to come to Ottawa to rule the country, and I am stirred to make these remarks by hearing the Premier of Ontario say that he did not care so much for his job as Premier of Ontario, only for one thing, namely, that he regarded it as an outpost in his keeping, and he bade the farmers of Ontario keep their eyes and their minds upon Ottawa. There, he pointed, was the field of their operations, and the province of Ontario will be kept as an outpost while a class or group, defying all the traditions of good Canadianism and all the desire that we have that we should blend our interests, will reject all these and say: We will keep the province as an outpost and make our assault upon our fellow citizens at Ottawa. As for the others-their day will come; labour, the professions, their day will come; the manufacturer, their day will come, their hour will come, in the language of my French friend. But now, just like a great storm blowing across the country, the farmers have announced that they are determined to sweep all before them.
Well, that is a magnificent way to proclaim the unity and solidarity of Canadianism. I sympathise with the Liberals that I see before me who are going down in this great storm. I do not suppose that two years hence Liberalism will be more than a name; and if the Conservative party, or that which shall succeed the Conservative party, does not defend the true national policy, which means Canada for the Canadians, a well developed and well balanced country, the Conservative party, or the party which succeeds it, will go down too.
Like the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. MOwat), I am wedded to no party, but I am wedded to a Canadian policy. I am wedded to the national policy, not to every feature oi it, because there have been mistakes; there have been injustices; but to the principle. Work at home, work together; buy at home; let your country be well balanced; then when time of trouble comes, you will be developed and able to take your part as in the late war, and when difficulties of a financial character arise, they will all be at home and you will not be paying out your gold to redeem yourselves and paying a huge discount to other nations. These things are too serious to trifle with, and I hope, in these crucial days, nobody is approaching these subjects except with the most acute concern.
