When the House rose for dinner I was calling attention to the question of exchange and inflation, and I shall not detain the House further than to make a general summing up. I will begin by congratulating the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria, the former leader of the Opposition, (Mr. McKenzie) on the courage and fortitude which he displayed in pronouncing unequivocally for Protection, in favour of Canada for the Canadians. It required some courage to do that in view of his surroundings, but I am pleased to see that he thinks more of Canada than of any party; the same spirit should inspire us all.
I just wish to say further with regard to the farmer that if any body asks why it is the farmer has become so aroused he will find the answer in the fact that the farmer dreads high wages, daylight saving, and things of that kind. Especially does he

dread shorter hours, and he cannot be blamed for that in view of his industrious life and its requirements. The question of shorter hours is no reproach to labour, because when we consider how it arose the answer at once presents itself. In the United States, for example, the operators of the coal mines, in order to have as little coal on hand as possible when the demand came for it, shortened the hours of production, so that if the worker in the coal mine was to have any pay at all he must necessarily shorten the hours of his working day so that he could get in more working days, because it frequently happened day after day and week after week that he would have not only many hours but whole days idle. Now when he sees that the operators have made tremendous profits, running all the way from 400 to 2,000 per cent, what can he do but strike? for neither this Government nor any other that I know of has provided him with any means of expressing his feelings in the matter except by striking? People when they read the newspapers hold up their hands in horror at the usurious perc ntage exacted by such operators as I have referred to, but they make no effort to stop it. The reason I refer to the United States is that the Americans have at last taken up this question in their usual strong and vigorous way. We in Canada, although I have nothing but the greatest respect for our Minister of Labour (Hon. Mr. Kobertson) who is I think a man of great energy and great ability and certainly of great sincerity, seem to be utterly confounded by these things. We have no solution; we offer no suggestions, and the cruel work goes on. Labour has therefore taken the matter into its own hands, and if we do not get an eight-hour day it will be because we will get a six-hour day, and the farmer will then be worse off than ever. If the manufacturers, for instance, decided to run the country, decided to form a powerful financial group and to concentrate their energies and their wealth, with all the ability that their leading men have, upon their own interests in this House, and with the farmers doing the same, where pray would the rest of Canada be? I would be just as strongly against the manufacturers in any such event as I would be against the farmers. We must be a united and a sane people, or we will cease to exist as a nation. I am confident that one of the difficulties this country labours under is that the people are largely uninformed except as to their own business, and here is a reproach 
that lies at the door of our leading men. Our ministers of government and the leading men of the Opposition might well go through the country, not at election times when nobody believes anybody else, but at other times, and explain the broad principles of government and of statesmanship. A statesman, Gladstone said, is a man who ascertains the facts and acts accordingly. In this way our leading men would learn in their peregrinations what the true conditions of the country were; they would know what the country thought and needed, and the country would know also what they thought; but at the present time, until the war drum of elections is sounded, nobody pricks up his ears about the country at all, and it is left to Canadian clubs and similar institutions to educate the country. This is a very serious drawback, and I am quite convinced that the good feeling as well as the intelligence of the country would be very much developed if our leading men were to visit different sections of the country at different times.
I want to touch for a moment upon a source of energy that has come like a flash into view and will afford us more comfort than anything else that I know of. The day of coal has gone by. Even if it could be mined, it is of poor quality or it is not there-I am referring to hard coal particularly, and the highest quality of soft coal. Gasolene has become so tremendously expensive that it is fast disappearing in public estimation and is creating a need which is about to be supplied, industrial chemists tell us, by industrial alcohol. The Americans a few years agb manufactured 6,000,000 gallons of alcohol per annum. Now they manufacture over 100,000,000 per annum. Our industrial alcohol, owing to the nervousness of the temperance people, has to be shipped from the distillers to Ottawa, there be denatured, and sent out to the users throughout the country. The consequence is that the freight alone is so expensive that Canada is put out of business as a consumer of industrial alcohol. That has to be stopped. The National Council of Industrial Research begs the Government to tell the people to grow more corn, and potatoes and everything of that sort' from which alcohol can be easily made, and then to take off all sorts of embargoes such as I have referred to, so that this source of energy may be made available to the people.
which means, of course, not only motive power but heat. We are short of electricity, and even if we had all the electricity we

wanted, alcohol has- become so cheap as a manufacturing product that one might almost describe it as the product of the wizard's wand. The hope of the world lies in industrial alcohol. Let us be alive to that fact and see to it that the Government duly recognizes it. A few years ago it was discovered that peat could be made into a fertilizer. I wrote to the department then, some five years ago, and begged them not to let some people get hold of all the peat bogs in the country and, after they had been tied up in this manner, find that they were all owned privately. I believe that some steps were taken in the matter. There is a fertilizer which, as the chemist might say, by a single twist of the wrist could be made available to the whole country, and surely it is necessary and desirable that this should be done.
I desire to say in closing-because it is a matter that is very near to my heart-that the basis of religion and morals is individual liberty; and when individual liberty is gone then no religion or morals can exist. The Creator recognized this truth, and He could not establish the moral law or be the fountain of that law and compel one single human being by means of prohibition or any such device. We are to have no freedom, no free will in anything, except by the behest of the prohibitionists. If you want Bolshevism, if you want that frightful explosion of energy which we saw in Russia, which overthrew like a volcanic eruption the tyrannical and autocratic system that was in vogue there, then that is the way to get it. There was no sense in the cruelty practised there by the ruling classes. The country did not belong to the people but to the few. How can we expect a great multitude, disturbed like an immense animal from its long sleep of oppression, to do otherwise than rise up and smash everything to pieces? Believe me, there is far more of that very spirit in this country than many people imagine, and it may show itself in many peculiar ways and not be recognized as the spirit of Bolshevism until it is too late. Why pray when the policeman is at the door? That is the motto of the prohibitionists and the user of force, the man who is substituting force for faith. Hail the policemaji! Crush them! Do what no divine plan ever did or could do, and you will show your human presumption, your ignorance and your incapacity. Let me say that no moral system can substitute the "must" for the "ought." In conclusion, let me extend in all sincerity the hand of fellowship from one province to another,
if I may be bold enough to do so. Surely the Protestant and the English speaking people have played some part in Quebec. Surely they have shown their faith in Quebec, as well as their high regard for the French people. We are the same as they; our interests are linked up with theirs; our prosperity and our whole future, in Ontario at least is linked up with that of Quebec. If Quebec and Ontario cannot pull together they will both be ruined, and Ontario knows this whether Quebec does or not. Now, we are all men and women, whether we are French or English, Liberals or Conservatives, farmers, manufacturers or mechanics. Let us drop the race cry; drop the party cry. Let us of course be loyal to whatever school of thought we belong to; let us be loyal to our friends within reason. But let us remember that above all things we are human beings and must be loyal to human liberty and human rights.
Mr. PIERRE F. CASGRAIN (Charle-voix-Montmorency):	Mr. Speaker, like
many others who have preceded me in this debate, I am glad to have the privilege of participating in the deliberations of this Parliament in these new buildings. Throughout the ages among all peoples a custom has prevailed of erecting monuments to commemorate the lives of great men and the occurrence of great and noteworthy events,-monuments designed to give to future generations a proper conception of the glory of their people. These new buildings which we have just entered, when they will have been finally completed, will stand forever as the best monument to the grandeur and magnificence of the Canadian people. Now, Mr. Speaker, although I join with others in pleasure at this fact, I must confess some disappointment with the speech from the Throne. We expected to hear much more from the Government in the way of new legislation intended to solve the problems of the day. In these new buildings to-day we are face to face with many questions of a very grave nature that demand immediate attention from the Government. Yet in the speech from the Throne there is nothing to indicate that the Government proposes very much in the way of progressive legislation. Mention is made of different events that have occurred since the last session, events concerning for the greater part the affairs of the people of Europe. We also have a reference to the International Labour Convention which was held in Washington last fall, but although there were delegates from our Government

at that convention, we do not hear in the speech from the Throne that our Government intends to introduce any new legislation in order to ameliorate the conditions of the labouring classes of this country. It is amusing to read such sentences as this, which appears in the speech from the Throne:
From every quarter of the world is being impressed, often by severe privation and suffering, the one great lesson that increased production through increased work, combined with thrift and economy in individual and State, is the only sure hope of business improvement and future prosperity.
Now, this is very nice indeed, if only the Government would make some attempt to put this theory into practice. This is a time when there is greater need than ever existed before for Parliament and people to co-operate in the task of working out a solution of the many problems which confront us. It is also pre-eminently a time for the exercise of proper caution when we embark upon untried policies. It is no time for pursuing false doctrines in grappling with political, social or economic problems. It is interesting to read in the speech from the Throne that the affairs of our country are in a very good state, that Canada has maintained a record of social order and industrial and commercial prosperity second to none. If, however, we go to the bottom of the question, as the member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. L. J. Gauthier) stated this afternoon, we shall find that, on the contrary, the affairs of Canada are in an absolutely unsatisfactory condition, due undoubtedly to the imprudence and improvidence of the present Government.
If business was so good in Canada why was the fifovernment obliged, a few days ago, to put an embargo on the selling of foreign securities on the markets of Canada, and to fix the prices of Victory Loan bonds, decreasing the price of those gilt-edged securities for which the Government said we would get par? Many financiers upon being apprised of this action, have expressed the opinion that this is one of the weakest steps that the Government could have taken in order to restore the financial condition of the country. It is bound to be misunderstood by people abroad and to prevent new business from coming to this country. It will also make it much more difficult for the Government to float further loans such as they have been launching in years past. When we contrast the way in which the affairs of the country were run a few years ago with the way in which they are run to-

day, we find that the people of Canada are just as much burdened and taxed as any people ever were. I believe, as a matter of fact, that we are more heavily taxed than the people in any other country. We pay municipal, provincial and federal taxes. The people are absolutely burdened with taxation and yet the Government, notwithstanding the increase in the cost of living, which is being further added to by this taxation, has not seen fit to place in the speech from the Throne any intimation that legislation is contemplated to alleviate the troubles of a suffering people. Either the Government is absolutely deaf to the voice of the people or the people are crying out in vain and their voice cannot reach the Government. When one looks at the treasury benches and contrasts the appearance that it presents to-day, with the appearance that it presented a few years ago, and when we remember the doings of the Government within the last few months, we may be inclined to believe that the spirit of the devil is not dead. We see the Government to-day trying to do things that have never been done before by any Government in any democratic country. Devilish deeds are being done by the Government to keep in power as long as they can and to prevent the people from passing judgment upon them. I say the spirit of the devil is not dead and I believe that the devil himself is.not dead.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

You are laughing, gentlemen, but we saw not long ago in Montreal the respectable, honourable, venerable Minister of Trade and Commerce, the present leader of the Government, addressing the Canadian Club, and we heard him telling the people of Montreal that the affairs of this country are not so bad after all, and that they should not listen to those people who tell them that we should have a change of government; that it would not do any good and that the only thing to do is to hold on and stick to the Government of the day. The leader of the Government said to the members of the Canadian Club, the leading people in the financial world in Montreal: "The only thing you have to do is to economise, work and produce more." We had heard that slogan before-economise and produce. But has the Government given any fair chance to the people to put this doctrine into practice? How can they economise when, since the beginning of the war and after the war, the Government has done everything it could to help the trusts and the big interests? Last year when there was

apprehension throughout the country as to the high cost of living and the abnormal conditions that had been created in Canada, a measure was introduced into this House and a Board of Commerce was created and given wide and broad powers. Its duty was to inquire into the different conditions of life, to try and set fair prices and to see that the big interests and the people controlling capital should not exact too much from the people. What have we seen and what has been the result of that board? After about five or six months trial I fail to see that any result has been brought about. Has it decreased or helped in any way to decrease, the prices of the commodities most necessary to life? Not at all. I believe that the prices are the same this year as they were last
They are higher.

And in some cases they are higher. We heard a few days ago that three of the big sugar refineries in Montreal had met together and that they had increased the price of sugar from one to three cents per pound. That is a fact that cannot be controverted. I have been told that this has been done under the supervision, and with the quasi consent, of the Board of Commerce that was created last year.
Mr. Speaker, this Board of Commerce has also conducted other inquiries in different parts of the country. We do not know the results of all those inquiries, but as regards the province of Quebec we may say that the inquiries were conducted-I would not say in an indifferent way, but in a manner that was not quite satisfactory. We have seen some companies ignore certain orders of the Board, and yet the Board seemed to be absolutely handicapped in the matter of bringing the recalcitrants to reason and compelling their submission to the orders.
And what do we see to-day, Mr. Speaker? Just before the opening of this session the press announced the resignation of the President of the Board-one of the most capable men that the Government saw fit to appoint to that position. Many rumours have been current regarding his resignation. Some are to the effect that it is on account of a misunderstanding with the Civil Service Commission, which did not want to see the Board working satisfactorily. That may be so; we do not know. Other rumours are to the effect that certain circumstances that the President of the Board did not want to disclose were responsible for the course he took. We are
assembled to-day, Mr. Speaker, to discuss national affairs and to try to adjust them in the best interests of all concerned. I put a question on the Order Paper, and so has the member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent), asking that all the correspondence leading up to the resignation be submitted to this House as soon as possible, and that an investigation be undertaken to ascertain the real reasons that brought about Mr. Justice Robson's retirement. I might add that we have also heard that his action might have been influenced by supposed friends of the Government who have differences to adjust with the Board. The people have a right to know every circumstance in connection with the resignation of the President to see whether such resignation was, if I may use the word, forced.
'The acting leader of the Government (Sir George Foster) when he visited Montreal and paraded as one of the devils of the Administration told us to produce more. If we are to credit the reports of the different industries and Boards of Agriculture in the several provinces, we must come to the conclusion that we have gone a long way towards increasing production in every line of agriculture and of commerce, and that at the present time our people cannot do very much more unless the Government cornea to their rescue and gives them a fighting chance and fair play.
I said, Sir, that our people cannot do very much more to-day unless the Government tells us fairly iwhat it intends to do regarding the fiscal policy of the country. We hear on every side that people are afraid to' put capital in any new enterprise because they are not sure what the Government is going to do next. In Montreal people have come to me and 'asked what was the intention of the Government regarding the Excess Profits War Tax; was it the intention to keep it in. force for another year? We have not .any explanation from the 'Government :as to their intentions. Last year we were told that a commission for the revision of the Tariff was to be appointed to inquire into conditions prevailing in this country, but up to now, so far as I know, we have not been advised that any such commission has been appointed. We hear that the Government is in possession of certain information, 'but that information is very vague and incomplete, and is not what was promised by the Prime Minister last year on the floor of this House.
I said at the opening of my remarks that the devil was not dead. One day we

see another devil of the Government represented by the unquestioning faith and optimistic personality of the President of the Privy Council, we see him telling the people of his constituency that everything is all right, and praising the Government for what it has been doing since the waT and iwhat it intends to do later. Mr. Speaker, it may be true that the President of the Privy Council is of the opinion that everything is all right with the business of this country, hut if he really entertains that opinion it must be based on very imperfect information of the affairs of this country. If that is the information given to him in his constituency, I would advise him to go into some of our big centres, where I aim confident he would be informed that conditions are not so satisfactory as he has 'been led to believe. He hears only one bell-the bell of the Union Government, and it is not the best bell to listen to in my opinion.
Mr. Speaker, it is no use to talk about the affairs of this country being thoroughly satisfactory and the people quite prosperous, and by way of confirmation to quote figures and statements as did the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. McGregor) who seconded the Address yesterday. There is a better way than that, and if I may use the words of a great statesman who is no longer with us, the late Bight Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurder, when he was leader of His Majesty's loyal Opposition I would say:
It Is no use quoting figures and statements to convince the people that they are happy and prosperous. When I shall have the direction of the affairs of Canada it will be my policy to enact such legislation as will bring happiness and success to everybody; it will not be necessary to quote figures and statements to realize you are happy and prosperous; you will feel it in your pocket.
The only way the people can he satisfied to-day and the trade and commerce of the country placed on a proper basis and so bring hack that national prosperity which we enjoyed from the year 1896 down to 1911 is by -an immediate readjustment of our fiscal policy.
We have, Mr. Speaker, on the other hand, as I said, another good devil of the Government-this is a real one, and I bow to him-the hon. member, the young and promising Minister of the 'Interior (M-r. Meighen). A few months a-go he came down as far as our old province of Quebec and addressed a meeting in the city of Quebec itself.
Then he told a big gathering of shoe manufacturers that they would have to be sub-

jected to further taxation; that if they made big profits the Government would try to get some of them. Two or three weeks later the same minister addressed a gathering of farmers in Winnipeg, and on that occasion he said: "Trust us; we will adjust matters so that you will have a moderate tariff, moderate protection; you will get what you want and be happy." That, Mr. Speaker, is not all. In an effort to appease the people, to keep them quiet, as an old schoolmaster would do with his class, the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) announced that an investigation would be made with a view to seeing what could be done with regard to the tariff. That investigation has been promised session after session, but it never seems to materialize. Now that the minister has officially assumed the duties of his office and is in his seat in the House, we hope that the inquiry with regard to the tariff will be instituted, so that we may know what the situation is and advise our constituents accordingly.
Mr. Speaker, among bad angels there sometimes happen to be a few good ones. Among the members of the Cabinet we find that there were three or four good ones. The former Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White); the former Minister of Agriculture (Hon. T. A. Crerar), and the former Minister of all Departments-I mean the member for Halifax (Hon. A. K. Mac-lean)-as good angels among the devils, separated from their colleagues, saying: "This is no place for us." Some people say that they are defaulters for leaving the Government, but as the member for.St. Hyacinthe (Mr. Gauthier) said this afternoon, these men entered the Government with a sincere desire to render service in a good cause, and when they considered that they had finished their work and done their duty, they withdrew. Possibly they were dissatisfied, too, with the manner in which public affairs were being administered. These gentlemen, who are public men of the highest character, having seen fit to resign on the ground that their work was finished, the Government of which they formed a part should immediately do the same-they should resign and appeal to the people. It is recognized in our constitution that a dissolution of Parliament is called for when public interest demands that the country should be consulted upon a question of great importance or when the ministers fail to obtain the support of the majority in the House. Never, I believe, in the history of Canada did public interest so strongly demand the resignation of the

Government and an appeal to the people. I need not go into the details of the formation of Union Government; they are known to every one. The Government was formed to win the war. No other policy was laid down at that time. I do not believe that the hon. gentlemen from this side who entered the Union Government would have done so had the carrying on of the war not been the only purpose of its formation. New problems have now arisen. It is impossible for most of the hon. gentlemen who. comprise the Union Government and who are either extreme free-traders or extreme protectionists to agree. The only solution of the difficulty is in appeal to the people.
There is another reason, Sir, why the Government should resign at once, and it must be obvious to every one. I do not wish to be disrespectful in referring to members of the Government, but it is a fact that we have to-day only a remnant of the Administration; and they do not represent the feeling and the sentiment of Canada. Moreover, if we are well informed, the ministers are wrangling among themselves on the question of who shall be Prime Minister or leader of the Government. The office of Prime Minister seems to have lost its usefulness in the affairs of Canada. We are told that the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) is critically ill and that he cannot return to his duties for some time. I want to be fair to the Prime Minister. He deserves credit for his services during the war and for the manner in which he did his duty to this country and to the Empire as well. But if he is as ill as people say he is, it is unfair for the ministers to try to force him to stay at the head of the Administration. It is unfair to Parliament, and it is unfair to the people. In such circumstances as these the Prime Minister should either resign his office or remain in full assumption of his duties, so that we may know where we stand. If he is not as ill as people say he is, he should be here to lead the Government and direct the affairs of the country. The Prime Minister is the pivot of the Government. All the other ministers may withdraw, but if he remains the Government still exists. When the Prime Minister disappears the Government falls. He has more real power than the King himself; only Parliament is above the Prime Minister. Everybody looks to the Prime Minister, not to his assistant or substitute, for the direction of the affairs of the country. I am speaking here to-day as a member of this Parliament, and I am criticising the present attitude of the Government of the
day, and the Prime Minister in that capacity, as well as in that of the representative of the county of Charlevoix-Montmorency, which I have the honour to represent in this House. We have the right to have the Prime Minister with us to-day instead of having dummies and substitutes and a bunch of green grocers, if I may be permitted to use that term, to administer the affairs of this country when matters come up that must be settled immediately. When I say that we should have the resignation of the Government and a dissolution of Parliament, I do not ask for something unusual or unprecedented. All other countries that have been at war have changed governments since the war; they have had elections, and nobody seems to have criticised them. If I am not mistaken, there was an election in England immediately after the war. Not a new Government, but practically the same Government was re-elected to conduct the affairs of that country after the war. The former Government had a war mandate and now they have a peace mandate. In France, what was dene? An election was held recently and a new Premier was elected. The former great Premier, Mr. -Clemenceau, who directed the destinies of France during practically the whole period of the war and who is justly called the " Father of Victory." has been denied the privilege of being President of the French Republic. What is the reason for that? Because the [DOT] people of France now realize that although this Premier was good for war; that he had all the capacity and energy to conduct the affairs of the country during the period of the war, his usefulness had passed; that new problems had arisen, that conditions had changed and that therefore, the Premier and the Government should also be changed. Why not do the same thing in this country, and then after an election we would know exactly where we stand?
We have been told in this Parliament as well as in the legislatures of the different provinces, that we are a democratic country administered by responsible Governments. If that be so in fact, surely, in order to live up to the traditions of England and also to preserve the rights and privileges that have been granted to us by the constitution, and which were acquired by our forefathers from the mother land, we should immediately go to the people of this country and obtain a new mandate, and a new Parliament ought to be chosen that would come to this House and be truly representative of the country at this time.

I said that public opinion must be at the back of the Government, but what do we find is the trend of public opinion to-day? If we look not only in the Chambers of the ministers at Ottawa and in certain of the provinces that are still backing the Government but throughout the country generally, -we find that the public opinion ot Canada ingoing against the Government. What is needed to settle the affairs of Canada at the present time?
The peace problem can be settled by peace and work only. The 9 p.m. peace which has been acquired with great sacrifices on the other side, the blood of our sons mingling with the blood of the sons of other nations, must give us life. To live we must work, and in order to work we must be willing and active. It is all very well for the Government to say to the people of Canada: Work; but the people can turn to the Government and say to them: Govern and administer and look after us. We must, in other words, have a government that will not have the weakness and the laissez faire and the laissez aller of the present Government, a government which, instead of conducting the affairs of this country, has rather been led by events and a desire to cling to the treasury benches and who believes that it can continue to hold on to them by its own will and its own consent.
/Before resuming my seat, I should like to make a few observations in reference to the speeches made this afternoon by certain hon. members. The hon. member for Park-dale (Mr. Mowat) in the course of his remarks intimated that Union Government was a mixture of the best elements of the Liberal and Conservative parties at the time when it was formed, and that there was no reason why Union Government should not go on. That may be so, but it is no reason why the Liberal party here to-day should not stand as it was in years past and as it is at the present time. The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Burnham) made certain remarks in which I cannot acquiesce. He said that for instance very soon, in a few years, the Liberal party would be a party of the past, and it might be also that the Conservative party would be a party of the past, and he looked at the new agrarian party and said: This is the party of to-day. Listening to the address of the hon. member for Peterborough West, we discover that he is, although I did not want to believe it until to-day, a very bad preacher, a false prophet and a pessimist. The hon. members who sit 
around me in this House remain Liberals as we were when we entered this House and we stand to fight for the good Liberal cause. I have been a Liberal for over ten years now, ever since I started to mingle in public affairs and politics, and I would not change to-day. A party that has produced such men as Blake, Mackenzie, the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the Hon. Mr. Mercier, the hon. leader of the province of Quebec, Fielding, Mackenzie King, is strong enough and good enough for me. Its policy that was advocated in the past and which has given to this country such years of great prosperity as we have seen from 1896 to 1911, a party which has given to this country fair representation and fair franchise and elections in years past, is a party of which every one ought to be proud, and as long as there remains a little bit of the flag of the old Liberal party flying anywhere in Canada, I shall be with it and I will stand and if needs be, fall to support it and I will call every one of the supporters of His Majesty's loyal Opposition, whether they are real Liberals or new members of the Agrarian party, our separated brothers of to-day, to join with us and support unanimously the amendment that was presented yesterday to the Address by the leader of the Opposition in order that it may be carried.

Have there been any defections from the ministry because of disagreement? Only one, so far as I know, and that .was when my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) resigned from the ministry over the Budget of last session. Has any other minister who has resigned said he disagreed with the Cabinet on their policies? I think not. If this were a discredited ministry would it be likely that the people of this country would advance to the Government such huge sums of money as they have done in the past few years? It is absolute poppycock to talk of the irresponsibility of fche Government and of a want of continuity of thought and action on the part of the ministers. It is very easy to talk like that, but facts are facts, and truth will prevail. What are the facts? My hon. friend accused the Government of instability and non-continuity of thought and action. What are good tests whether a country is prospering or not? Prices are a fairly good test. Prices for practically every commodity are high. Money by common consent is said to be plentiful. Times are good.
There is very little idleness. Our factories are busy and our manufacturers, that from one end of the country to the other, tell us they cannot find enough of commodities to fill the orders they have. Consequently the workmen are employed. Our bank deposits are increasing month by month, and that fact can be taken as fairly good evidence as to the conditions which exist in the country at the present time. I admit that there is unrest; everyone knows that there is. But let us be fair with the people and with ourselves. Have hon. gentlemen opposite mentioned any single thing that can be said to be a cause of the unrest? If there is a cause let us know what it is that we may endeavour to remove it. But do not let hon. gentlemen simply get up and with carping criticism condemn the Government wholesale because the Government cannot do the impossible.
I am firmly convinced that there are more causes than one for the present unrest, which is by no means confined to Canada. The cause is partly an economic one, but it is psychological as well. The whole world is abnormal to-day, and Canada has unfortunately not escaped the common fate. Any one who is tolerably acquainted with history knows, and it can be proven, that after every convulsion such as we have just

experienced there have prevailed conditions similar to those which exist at the present time. One hundred years ago, after the Napoleonic Wars, the exchanges of the world were against Great Britain just as they are to-day; not ten per cent or twenty per cent, but forty per cent, and for the identical causes to which are to be attributed the state of exchange at the present time. Following the American Civil War the same conditions prevailed in the United States as prevail there to-day. And so it is throughout history. As our civilization becomes more complex, and as we harness the forces of nature in order to help us develop that complex civilization, the more difficult will be our problems. No government can obviate these conditions, and it is well to realize the fact and face the situation as best we can. We must understand that the high cost of living is not peculiar to Montreal or Toronto, to the province of Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, or to the Dominion of Canada as a single country. It is not even confined to the belligerent nations, for if you turn to the neutral countries you will find that the cost of living is greater in those places than it is in the countries that were at war. Now, these are not idle statements. The press of the world will convince you of their truth. For instance, in Spain, a country which never drew the sword at all, the cost of living is higher than in Great Britain; and in the Scandinavian countries, which sold their goods by the million to belligerent nations, you will find that the cost of living is higher than in the United States. I do not make these statements merely for the sake of having something to say, because they can be substantiated. In South America, where there are countries that never sent a man to the war, the very same conditions prevail. The unrest is universal. That being so, what justification can there be for any censure of our Government? Let us be fair, however much we may be critical. I do not say that the Government is infallible. I quite realize that the Government is human like the rest of us and has made mistakes, as it will probably make mistakes in the future. But I reiterate, let us be fair; let us give them a chance to carry on the affairs of the country until times improve. There is only one remedy for the condition that is disturbing the world to-day-I care not whether it is in the Argentine, in Stockholm, London, Paris or Ottawa-and that remedy is the one suggested in the speech from the Throne, a remedy that existed since the moral law was first established

amongst men. That remedy consists in thrift and economy and home purchase, and unless we apply it, the same conditions will exist a year hence as exist to-day.
But the leader of the Opposition, whom I am glad now to see in his seat, did not confine himself in his criticism to home affairs. He went abroad and criticised this Government in regard to its foreign policy. Now, Mr. Speaker, Canada has passed the stage of her swaddling clothes and become a nation, and the Canadian people and Parliament must cease from thinking provincially. We must think in a national and an international way; the day has passed when purely provincial problems shall engage our attention. We won by right a place in the greatest Peace Conference that mankind has ever held. We won recognition by the shedding of the good red blood of our men, and by their magnificent bravery in the field, and we therefore have the right to stand side by side with the greatest nations on earth. I therefore deprecate any attempt on the part of hon. gentlemen to belittle Canada and speak disparagingly of its foreign affairs. When they lo so they show a lack of appreciation of the part which the people of this country played in the great war, and such derogatory criticism of Canada's status is little-Canadianism. What have we accomplished? In fifty years we have created a great nation, connected East and West; established a vast system of transportation; dredged our harbours; opened up a great system of lake and river transportation; created great manufacturing industries; and developed in this country the most highly skilled artisans that are to be found anywhere, a fact which was amply demonstrated in the war. From a peace basis we suddenly entered on war conditions and engaged in the manufacture of shells by the same concerns that had formerly made farming implements. We have placed Canada upon the map of the world. Our banking institutions are going abroad for business and expect our manufacturers to follow. And they will follow. We took our place at the Peace Conference and the Labour Conference, anl before this session of Parliament is over, I understand, legislation will be brought forward to give us a status at Washington with a representative there. This is as it should be, Mr. Speaker, and for my part I shall not be satisfied until we have a representative of Canada in every port of the world where we can secure
a dollar's worth of trade. If we are to take our place properly amongst the nations of the world we must think in terms of diplomacy and realize that we need representatives in foreign countries; and instead of criticising the Government in regard to its foreign policy it would be well for the Opposition to lend some aid in carrying it out.
My hon. friend wants an amendment to the Election Act. Why does he desire this? Because Quebec is not represented in the Cabinet; that is the one reason. Now, why is Quebec not represented in the Cabinet? How many members from the province of Quebec were returned to support the Government? Three out of sixty-five. How many of these three hold seats in the Cabinet? Two. And where is the other? Representing Canada in Europe. Is this Government to be blamed because Quebec has no greater representation I should think not. But they were not satisfied with that. They went to Quebec and made the Hon. Mr. Blondin Postmaster General with a seat in the Senate. The leader of the Opposition says that Mr. Blondin does not represent the people of Quebec because he was defeated in two constituencies. Mr. Speaker, is Mr. Blondin the only man who was ever defeated in two constituencies and who seeks to advise the House. The hon. gentleman who holds the position of leader of the Opposition was himself defeated in North Waterloo and North York, and he comes and tells us we should have a new election, when he could not obtain a seat at all in his own province nor in Quebec, nor in New Brunswick nor Nova Scotia. Where did he get his seat? In Prince Edward Island. And this is the source from which we get the advice that we should have an election! I do not want to be personal, but I do plead for fairness, and my hon. friend has no more reason to suggest that we should have an election than- the man who has not a seat in the House at all. He says that an election should be held because Parliament has outlived its mandate. What does it mean to say that Parliament has outlived its mandate? Is Parliament elected for any particular term other than was provided for in the constitution? The constitution says that Parliament shall be elected for five years. Is there anything in theory or practice that would change that term? I have not heard of it. If there is, I would like to know it, because I am interested in these things.

Is there any other reason he advanced? The Opposition desire it. Did you ever see an Opposition that did not desire an election? The Opposition has no responsibility to the public and it does not need any policy. It devotes itself to lambasting the Government. That is the duty of an Opposition, and that is what it is generally engaged in doing.
Does the press of this country demand an election? Is there any considerable section of the sane press of Canada asking for an election at this time? The press is a very good indication of what the people are thinking. Are the people who direct the policies of the great papers asking for an election? Are the men who write the editorials in our papers asking for an election? No. Why? Because they are sane, straightforward, thinking, Canadians who know that if an election was held it would disorganize this country. What we want is steadiness and to give the people a chance to get down to work again in order that the psychological conditions may become normal.
And the Opposition.

The Opposition, 1 hope, will become normal, although that is perhaps too much to hope for. Do the farmers want an election? No. How do I know? Because a congress of about a thousand farmers was held the other day in Saskatchewan and some one in that body submitted ,a resolution asking that this Government be called upon to resign. Did they adopt it? No. The farmers do not ask for an election. That is just a sign of the times. Do the people want an election? Is there in this country anywhere a concerted mass of opinion which demands an election? If there is I want to know it, and I fancy the Government want to know it. I defy the leader of the Opposition, or any of the men who follow him, to name any considerable block of public opinion in this country that is at the present time demanding an election.
What about policies? This Government, the leader of the Opposition says has no policy. Has he a policy to put before this country? I have not heard of it. How about the trade policy? I believe that the next campaign in this country will be fought on the question of the tariff, which is a good, clear-cut, straight issue. Where do my hon. friend and his friends stand on that question? Are they a unit on the tariff question? No. How about free trade and direct taxation, amongst the men from the West? How about adequate protection,

with my distinguished friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie)? And how about St. James division, Montreal, to-day, where there are two Liberals running, one as a straight Liberal and the other as a Liberal-Protectionist? Whoever heard of a Liberal-Protectionist?
The leader of the Opposition said that this Government is unpopular. One of the things I glory in is that we had a government elected to do unpopular things and that it has done them. Why is it unpopular? Because it took the boys from the home-some of them unwilling homes-and sent them to the front; it told the people what they would eat; it told the people what they would drink-
What they would not drink.

Or what they would not drink; it told the newspapers what they would print and what they would not print, and it told the newspaper writers what they would write and what they would not write. Can a government be popular and do these things? Of course it cannot. This Government was not elected to do popular things; it was elected to do unpopular things, and I glory in its consistency. I am sure that the Canadian people who elected this Government to do unpopular things will stand behind these men who have fought the good fight.
The unkindest cut of all from the man who leads the Opposition, and who some day hopes to sit in the seats of the mighty and to lead the Government of this country as Prime Minister, is when he attacks the present Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) because he is away seeking health. Could partisanship go farther?

I am sure my hon. friend would not wish consciously to misrepresent my attitude. If my remarks yesterday were in any way capable of the interpretation which he is placing upon them, or if by any turn they would lend themselves to such an interpretation, I am extremely sorry. Nothing was further from my thought than that I should reflect in any way on the Prime Minister. When I spoke of the desirablility of the Prime Minister being in his seat to speak of matters of policy, I had reference to the principles underlying parliamentary government. I was speaking of the desirability if possible of having the leader of the Government in the House to deal with matters of public policy. The reference was followed immediately by a remark in regard to the Prime

Minister's health in which I said that 1 shared the feeling of regret of everyone in the House that the Prime Minister was not able to take his seat. I was glad to-day to hear that the Prime Minister is so much better that he hopes to be back in this House again before very long. I cannot be too emphatic in saying that any reference that was made to the Prime Minister in that connection was made to the office of the Prime Minister and not to Sir Robert Borden who happens unfortunately to be prevented from being in the House at this time.

I am not only glad to give my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) an opportunity of making that explanation, but I am extremely glad to hear it from his own lips. My hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) in extenuation of the impression that had been made by the leader of the Opposition yesterday took occasion this afternoon to refer to the incident. I do not wish to impugn the motives of any man or to put wrong words in his mouth, but I have looked at the resolution and I am going to read one or two words from it. I accept without reservation the statement of my hon. friend, but in justice to myself I desire to quote this sentence. In the amendment which my hon. friend moved and which my hon. friend from Cape Breton seconded he regretted the "protracted absence of the Prime Minister, the widely accepted belief that it is not his intention to return to the duties of his office." I took it from that that he was not expected to return by my hon. friend and his friends and that they were trying to force him out of public life. I felt indignant, but I am glad to have the explanation from my 'hon. friend and I accept it. I hope the right hon. the Prime Minister will return soon in the full flush of health. Of the Prime Ministers who led Governments from the beginning of this war in other belligerent and allied countries, in so far as I know, there were only two living and in office at the end of the war and of these two one has since died. I refer to General Botha, the Prime Minister of South Africa. The other man is the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, our Prime Minister, who has carried a giant's load all these years, and who now, after four or five years of Herculean effort, is broken in health and has gone away for a brief respite from the onerous duties which bear heavily upon him as Prime Minister of this country. I am sure that I voice the sentiments of hon. members on both sides, Mr. Speaker, when I express the hope that he 6
will return, and return in good health this session. But whether he does or not, I am satisfied that the great majority of our people hope that he will stay away until his health is completely restored.
Now, Mr. Speaker, whether this Government wins or loses in the next campaign is in the lap of the gods, but whatever happens I am satisfied, as one of the members of this House and as a supporter of this Government, that Union Government has justified its existence. And, furthermore, I believe that when the work of this Government has been properly placed before the people it will stand a better chance of securing a majority of the seats in this House than any group existing at the present time, including that which is presided over by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition.
Mr. J. E. S. E. d'ANJOU (Rimouski) (translation): Mr. Speaker, I shall first take up some remarks which the hon. member from the Yukon (Mr. A. Thompson) just made. The hon. gentleman fervidly upheld the Government, and it is no wonder because it is owing to this fatherly Government for which he pleaded with so much force that he is privileged to hold a seat in this Parliament. So the people can understand why the hon. member who just resumed his seat was upholding with so much assurance, if not with great conviction, the moribond Government that are still the arbiters of the future of this country.
The hon. member from the Yukon found fault with the hon. leader of the Opposition for not having in his remarks touched upon the tariff question. My experience in public life has been short, still it seems to me that the Government, not the opposition, is called upon to draw up a political program. Last session, the Government named a commission which was to investigate tariff matters. The commission was to report so that the question could be settled during this session. In the Speech from the Throne there is nothing to show that the commission has done anything. Like every commission created by this Government, that commission did nothing and nothing has been put before the cabinet. As I said, it is the duty of the Government to outline a policy, and the leader of the Opposition is not bound to show his hand. While touring the country and specially the Maritime provinces, the leader of the Opposition had occasion to state his policy in



that connection, and that policy is known not only to the members of this House, but to the whole country. When the Government sees fit to raise that question,, the leader of the Opposition and all those who are proud to follow his lead will be here to uphold the Liberal programme which always was that of the people and opposed to the program of trusts and combines which is that of the Government now swaying the destinies of Canada.
The hon. member from the Yukon said that the leader of the Opposition regretted that the province of Quebec was unrepresented in the Canadian ministry. Sir, that province is not represented, and somuch the better. For my part, I venture to state that I do not wish that the province of Quebec should have representatives in such an administration. It will be represented when the people is called upon to bring the Government to trial and when a Liberal administration rules this country. At that time, when the people has faith in the Government, when the country is led by honest and enlightened men who do not wage their political battles against the province of Quebec, who do not make the most of racial and religious prejudices in order to remain in power, we shall be proud of seeing representatives of that province in such a Government.
From 1896 until 1911,, the province of Quebec was represented, and legally represented, in the Canadian administration, for we had as leader of this country the greatest man who ever lived in Canada, the one who has departed and whose memory shall live forever, the one who inspires the present leader of the Liberal party and his followers. When we have a Government of that stamp to head us, a Government composed, I shall not say of men as worthy as Laurier,, but of men who strictly adhere to his political principles, his respect for every race and every creed, of men who will avoid offending not only the one province, but any province in the Dominion of Canada; then, gentlemen, we shall be proud of being represented in such a cabinet.
Some contend that the hon. Mr. Blondin represents the province of Quebec, as a member of the Government. Some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have stated that the hon. Mr. Blondin had been defeated in the province of Quebec, only because of his having supported the Government enforcing the Conscription Act. That is not the only reason. He was

defeated, because, along with many others, in 1911 he had outrageously misled and deceived the people of that province.
The hon. member for the Yukon, who is always at the fore to defend the cause of the administration, sang the deeds of the boys at the front. Now that the war is over,, and that peace has come in, it were high time that a stop were put to that music which grates on our ears. The winning of the war was the Government cry to remain in office or to get a new lease of power; they should like to keep up that war cry and that the war were still going on. It served so useful a purpose for the hon. gentlemen that the war should go on. Unfortunately for them and happily for the people the war is concluded and I hope that a majority of votes will be cast in favour of the amendment so that- the Government may be forced to the country. On the Opposition side, we want the people appealed to, without the least fear as to result; we want the people freely to choose their representatives; we want the country to come back to British institutions, to responsible Government; we want the liberties that have been secured to us to be respected.
During the war, all laws and rights were suspended and crying abuses crept in. The present Government was the first to infringe the law, and not so long ago, our prisons were crowded with young men who had not reported for duty, and they were thrown into prison, because it was contended that they had violated the law. The guilty parties are the hon. gentlemen opposite. Those axe the men who should be packed like sardines in jail, and not these young men who often acted through ignorance or because they considered that it was better for the country that they should stay behind and remain steadily at work on their farms, to increase the production of foodstuffs, for our own people and our soldiers overseas.
Although the debate is nearing its conclusion, think it my duty to congratulate the mover and seconder of the Address who have so well discharged the task entrusted to them. But I cannot extend my congratulations to the Government itself, the Government has once more ignored the rights of the French language, a fault which has grown into a habit. At the opening sitting of the session, it is true, the Acting Prime Minister was kind enough to say a few words in French; but neither the mover nor the seconder of the Address have said a single word in French. The right hon.

the Acting Prime Minister in referring to the amendment moved by the leader of the Opposition queried whether it was not a fine bit of strategical camouflage. Let me tell him that it was his remarks in the French language, at the opening of the session, that could be styled a fine bit of camouflage; for, had he been honest, he wields enough influence over the Cabinet, as he is the substitute of the Prime Minister, to make his followers realize that the rights of the French language should be respected in this Parliament and that the mover or seconder of the Address should at least be able to express themselves in French. This is the third occasion on which I register my protest in this House in the name of my constituents. It is not enough to make speeches in French, but the constitution must also be respected. The two languages are' official and the rights of the French should be upheld. The mover or seconder of the Address, under the tradition, has always been a French Canadian or at least a Canadian conversant with the French language. Moreover, during the preceding sessions, I availed myself of the opportunity of saying that there is an hon. gentleman on the Government side who is fully qualified to move or second the Address in French. The hon. member from Edmonton (Mr. Maekie) is quite competent perfectly to perform that task. He has shown himself proficient in Parliamentary oratory, and is eminently gifted in the art of expression in the French language. Were the Government anxious to respect the rights of the French language, they could have, this year, entrusted him with the task of moving or seconding the Address.
From the very opening of the session, all the talk is about national unity and a better understanding; about making love and offering incense to Quebec.
In 1917, Quebec was not coaxed. The main thing was to win an election. The Unionist government saw fit to enforce conscription in order to discredit that province in the eyes of the other provinces, to get them at loggerheads with her and so to win the election and remain in power. It is two late now to cajole Quebec. They see to-day that they cannot be elected without the help of our province, and after vilifying her and treating her in the most outrageous manner, they are intent in making peace with her for political purposes. Well, Sir, Quebec is beautiful, great, noble in her loneliness. There is peace in that province; her government has assured prosperity to her people who live happy. The fault is Gi
not ours if the other provinces do not enjoy the same conditions.
It is rather late to flatter Quebec for, I repeat it, during the political campaign of 1917, that province has been used as a scape-goait; everywhere they have fanned the racial and religious prejudices and roused the other electors against her. It has been said: Quebec will not do her duty; the French Canadians refuse to enlist; conscription must be imposed upon them.
Sir, the French Canadians have too chivalrous an ancestry to warrant such aspersions, and the 22nd regiment have distinguished themselves overseas. For the third time I shall say that in Rknouski county we have two Victoria crosses, lieutenants Brillant and Raeble who were killed in action. We are not the descendants of cowards but of a chivalrous race. We wanted to fight, but freely, as men. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said in the electoral campaign that if the Government had been sincere, if they had used the necessary means to boost voluntary enlistment, conscription could have been dispensed with. Moreover, in other British Colonies, in Australia, for example, one of the most important colonies after Canada, conscription has been pooh-poohed. Consequently, it is neither more nor less than a political game against the Liberal party, in order to rouse the other provinces against Quebec with a view to remaining an power.
The address is particularly interesting for what it omits mentioning. The only important thing found in it is the plan of a new Franchise Act, It is obvious that the Government are not at all anxious to go to the people, but they are cautiously feeling their way. Why should we not keep the old Franchise Act, the one we had before the war? Owing to the war-time Elections Act, the country is spending monstrous amounts and, if I am not mistaken, the government have decided to maintain the system of enumerators in the making of the electoral lists which were previously the work of the municipal councils, the said lists being used for the federal as well as the provincial elections. They were fair and just to everybody and the country had nothing to pay. But, with the present system of enumerators,' those lists cost enormous sums of money, and besides they favour all kinds of frauds which profit to government candidates. I hope therefore that the Government will not exceed the bounds of decency and that if they introduce in the House a Franchise Bill its

principle will be more acceptable than that embodied in the War-time Elections Act and that all those entitled to vote shall have their names on the lists.
In the elections of 1917, a great number of citizens who for twenty years past had exercised the franchise, were denied their rights under the War-time Elections Act, because they were suspected of being opposed to the Government of the day. If the Government earnestly wish to put an end to the unrest in the country, they are bound to enact a Franchise Bill which is fair to everybody; they are hound to go to the people at once in order that the electors of Canada may choose their own representatives.
I am satisfied that when the people pass sentence on the present Government they will 'be anxious to appoint another one which better safeguards the country's interests, that is a Liberal government, worthy of the Canadian nation and the Liberal party, 'as the one we have had from 1896 to 1911, for the happiness and prosperity of the people.
Besides, the present Government have never represented public opinion. It is no use to say that the Unionist Government were elected to win the war-such was and is still their claim-but these gentlemen have no right to say that they have a mandate from the people, for this mandate was juggled away from them by means of the law of Elections in War time -and of the manipulation of the soldiers' vote overseas. I therefore say that the iGovernment have no right to say to the country and to the House that they have the support of the people, that they were elected to win the war iand to save the Empire. If the Government are so confident in the success of their 'administration, if they are so sure that the people are behind them, why do they not appeal to the people, why do they not go and ask them for a renewal of their mandate, not by means of an election that may be juggled away as in 1917, but in an election carried on as they were in 1896 and 1911, when the people were free 'to express their opinion on the choice of their representatives? When the Government decide to go before the people II .am sure of the verdict that they will obtain, and the Government themselves, well .aware of what that verdict would be, will do every thing 'to defeat the amendment proposed by the leader of the Opposition.
I. said a moment ago that 'there is unrest *in the country, an unrest largely due to the present Administration, but also to the high

cost of living. During last session, dt seems to me, a commission was .appointed to inquire into the high cost of living,, to examine how to remedy the situation; but unfortunately nothing has been done by this commission. The most efficient remedy with which the Government might meet the high cost of living would be overproduction and the lowering of the duty on agricultural machines and on all the articles needed by .the farmer. Overproduction is being all the time preached to the farmer; he is everywhere begged to produce and produce always but he is not given the means to produce any more than he does. Were the Government sincere, they would amend the tariff, they would modify it so as to relieve from duty all agricultural implements and all articles of first necessity to the farmer. In this way the farmer could produce more and at much less expenditure, and the consumer would benefit thereby. It seems to me quite important that- the Government should, during the present session, take measures to change 'the situation, to lower the cost of living; and this could be done by an intensive production, fostered, I repeat it, by a lowering of the duties on the agricultural implements and on the articles of first necessity to the farmer.
I would like, by the way, to say a word about the dismissals which are at present taking place in the 'Printing Bureau. As you know, employees .are being dismissed by fifties at least in the Printing Bureau. The reason given is 'that their services are not required and after these men are gone, longer hours are in certain offices imposed upon those that remain. If it is necessary to increase the working hours it must mean that these men were not useless. I have been told that these men were French Canadians, were old men, and that they were thrown on the street without pension, without any .compensation. This surely cannot be called measures of patriotism. As every one knows, the Government hardly practise economy; they spend lavishly, too lavishly even. Why not keep these men in the Printing Bureau? The Government pretend that these employees were dismissed for reasons of economy. If they were sincere let them begin by practising economy themselves. I .protest with energy against these dismissals.
Now, why have Americans been called here to effect a reclassification of the Civil Service? You remember that in 1911, the slogan of the opponents of the Liberal party, the slogan of the Tories, was, "No truck,

no trade with the Yankees". And yet, today, when anything or anybody is needed,, the Government apply to the United States, when we can have here what is needed, when we have Canadians who can do the work with as much intelligence and 'at less cost to the country. When this reclassification was to be made, why were not the chiefs of the departments taken to do it; they knew the situation much better than the Americans called to do the work and to whom fabulous sums were paid for the insignificant labour 'they have performed. I protest against this .abuse.
II again protest against the dismissals I have referred to, and |I hope that the Government will at least see to it that the men thus turned out be treated with justice. Old men of sixty, of seventy, were discharged; I hope that the Government will come 'to their help and will grant them such pensions as they deserve.
Before concluding, I would like to answer some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) and by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat), concerning the Liberal party. The hon. member for Parkdale used to be a Liberal, he bears a great name, that of a great Liberal, but I see that he has degenerated and he does not honour that name to-day. He stated that the Liberal party existed no more, that is was extinct in this country and that true Liberals could be found, not on your left, Mir. Speaker, but among those who crossed over to the other side and who are supporting the Government to-day.
The Liberal party is just as alive here as it is in Great Britain and the hon. member for Parkdale must have heard, a few days ago, of the splendid victory won by -the leader of that party in England, Mr. Asquith, in the constituency in which he was nominated for election. He too had been cast -aside because he had refused to compromise on the question of Liberal principles and because he would not follow Lloyd George and enter the coalition. He stayed away, but, to-day, the English Liberals who are just as true to their principles as we are to ours here, rejoice over his return to the British Parliament; I hope he will make it as hot for the coalition Government as the hon. leader of the Opposition has -started to do as regard this Government.
In closing, I must say that I support entirely the amendment introduced by the hon. leader of the Opposition. If the Government feel that they have a record worth
submitting to the people, if they ,are so sure of their re-election, why do they not go and face courageously the electors? Why do they not ask the Governor General for the dissolution of Parliament, in order to submit immediately their political record to the people? Personally, I am anxious for it, because we would be able to again demonstrate to the people of Canada that the hope and future welfare of this country are still with the Liberal party and the leader it selected in the great convention, held in August 1919. That -convention at which the hon. member for Prince was elected as leader, was really democratic, because all the different parts of the country were represented thereat.
With so distinguished a leader, ia loyal disciple -of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the bearer of a great name, and -a descendant of a proud -and noble stock, I a-m convinced that when we shall go before the people, they will recognize their true friends once more and place at the head of the country the eminent leader of the Liberal party, who, I am sure, will do justice to the Province of Quebec and restore in our country the happiness and prosperity which we emjoyed from 1896 to 1911.
On motion of Mr. L. J. Papineau (Beau-harnois), the debate was adjourned.

speechtext:
I lay on the
Table copies of communications that passed between myself and the Chairman of the Board of Commerce in connection with the resignation of the chairman. The correspondence is as follows:
Board of Commerce of Canada.
Ottawa, 23rd February, 1920. My Dear Sir George.
It is impossible for me to continue further in the office of Chief Commissioner of the Board of Commerce. I trust the Government will select a successor at an early date. This may be treated as a formal resignation if you so wish or I will 6end a more formal document.
As I previously informed you I could not see my way to removing my home to Ottawa and I am under the necessity of returning to

Winnipeg at once. Under these circumstances I should make way for another appointment.
Sincerely yours,
H. A. Robson.
The Right Hon.
Sir George E. Foster, P.C., G.C.M.G.
Board of Commerce of Canada.
Ottawa, February 23, 1920. The Rt. Honourable
Sir George E. Foster, P.C., G.C.M.G.,
Ottawa.
My dear Sir George,
My short experience on the Board of Commerce in the administration of The Combines and Fair Prices Act, has led me to views which make it improper for me to hold a position on that Board. The fact is that I am out of sympathy with the Act, and it is my duty to inform you thereof.
The general idea was that the Act was calculated to reduce the cost of living. That impression was largely erroneous. The primary idea of the Act was control of profits on sale of necessaries. To some extent that might affect the cost of living, but high prices and small profits may and in fact do very often coincide.
It is only the thoughtless that imagine that prices should have been brought down and that such was the function of the Board.
The economic policy of the country should be towards high prices and against low prices. Numerous governmental agencies, at the expense of the people of Canada, are doing their best to get the highest world prioes for Canadian produce. In view of this, any machinery to reduce prices of this produce is simply abortive.
But taking the Act as merely profit regulating, in my View it is largely fruitless, also because of the fact recited above, that the producer will find the highest market and the highest profit, and if these are abroad he will send his goods there. Once again I remark that the governments encourage him to do so.
It is futile to think of trying to bring down prices or profits on necessaries in view of above facts.
Dealing with it as a measure to repress profiteering, I have further objection to the Fair Prices part of The Combines and Fair Prices Act (which is the important part of that Act) in that it picks out for profit regulation those classes of producers and traders who deal in the necessaries of life. This regulation does not apply to the great number of other branches of business and occupation. We restrain and discourage the citizen who supplies food and clothing but leave free to profiteer as he pleases the man who deals in nonessentials, or luxuries. We do not touch any excessive charging for service involving mechanical or professional experience. There can only be one effect, i.e., to discourage persons from entering into the production and distribution of the necessaries of life.
There is, to my mind, further objectionable discrimination in- that the measures for controlling the selling prices of the retailer are in terms fairly effective, while those for reaching the manufacurer are not so.
A profiteering measure to reach the distributing class should, in my opinion, be local in its character and be administered locally. Federal machinery cannot reach the grievance effectually throughout all Canada.
[Sir George Foster.)
It seems to me further that the Act actually contains a provision which removes the last chance the consumer had to do anything for himself in reducing the cost of living. There never was before the Act anything to prevent a group of consumers from co-operating in the purchase of necessaries. They took their chance of being able to buy. But a declaration of parliamentary policy crept into the Act, and a manufacturer or wholesaler is not bound to sell to classes who were not accustomed to purchase from such manufacturers and wholesalers. This was designed to head off cooperative movements, which were likely to make progress for the benefit of consumer members and, as I say, restricted a remedy which elsewhere has been of some effect in price control.
I might also add1 that I think the provincial authorities should have been left with power to prosecute combines in any case where they might see fit, without being bound to first apply for a finding of the Board. The inquisitorial provisions of the Act, while of a nature useful in war time for ascertainment and control of food supplies and other necessaries, do not, in my opinion, fit ordinary conditions and only harrass and discourage business men.
I do not wish to be understood as saying that I do not think there is a legitimate and useful field for the Board of Commerce. Great good can be accomplished by the spread of information and by careful administration of investigating machinery. Publicity itself as to the reasonableness of cost and profit will to a substantial extent benefit the consumer. He may thereby know at least whether or not he is being imposed on. My idea is that a Federal body of general character working in with provincial authorities who would enforce anti-profiteering laws would be beneficial. But that is a matter which requires discussion and some re-casting of the Acts. My opinion of them as they now stand is stated above.
I am, yours sincerely, H. A. Robson.
Prime Minister's Office, Canada.
Ottawa, Ont., Feb. 25, 1920.
My dear Judge Robson,-I beg to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 23rd February, in which you say it is impossible for you to continue further in the office of Chief Commissioner of the Board of Commerce and ask that your resignation may be accepted at once. I have brought the matter before Council and an Order was passed to-day, accepting your resignation. Let me express personally my regret that you have found it, for reasons expressed in your letter, impossible to remain any longer in the position of Chief Commissioner or member of the Board.
Yours faithfully,
George E. Foster,
Acting Prime Minister. Hon. H. A. Robson, K.C.,
Board of Commerce,
Ottawa.
Ottawa, Ontario,
February 26, 1920.
Dear Judge Robson,-I beg to acknowledge your letter of the 23rd February, in which you give yeur views as drawn from your experience in the operation of the Board of Commerce ad-

ministration and your suggestions as to v-r.at might he done in the way of amendments to make the machinery more workable and to tetter effect the purposes had in view when the Board of Commerce Act was passed ny Parliament. I thank you for the suggestions, which will be carefully considered by the Government.
Tours faithfully,
George E. Foster,
Acting Prime Minister. Hon. H. A. Robson, K.C.,
Board of Commerce,
Ottawa.
